item.research_question: How can shifting alloy design from single-phase equiatomic to dual- or multiphase non-equiatomic configurations with controlled phase instability enable the joint activation of multiple strengthening and toughening mechanisms to achieve superior strength–ductility combinations?
item.material_system: 3d transition-metal non-equiatomic HEAs including Fe80−xMnxCo10Cr10 (x = 30–45 at.%), Co20Cr20Fe40−yMn20Niy (y = 0–20 at.%), and interstitially alloyed variants like Fe49.5Mn30Co10Cr10C0.5
item.processing_route: Vacuum induction melting followed by hot-rolling at 900°C with 50% thickness reduction, homogenization at 1200°C for >2 h with water quenching, cold-rolling to ~60% reduction, and annealing at 900°C for 3–60 min to control grain size and phase fractions
item.test_conditions: Room temperature tensile testing; microstructural characterization via XRD, EBSD, ECCI, APT, and TEM; thermodynamic calculations using Calphad at 300 K
key_findings: The Fe50Mn30Co10Cr10 dual-phase alloy exhibits significantly higher strength and ductility than single-phase variants due to the TRIP effect and massive solid-solution strengthening.
Adding 0.5 at.% carbon to Fe50Mn30Co10Cr10 yields Fe49.5Mn30Co10Cr10C0.5 with ultimate tensile strength up to nearly 1 GPa and total elongation of ~60%.
The interstitially alloyed Fe49.5Mn30Co10Cr10C0.5 shows twice the tensile strength of the equiatomic Co20Cr20Fe20Mn20Ni20 reference while maintaining identical ductility.
In Fe50Mn30Co10Cr10, annealing at 900°C for 60 min increases FCC grain size from ~4.5 μm to ~17.5 μm and causes nonmonotonic variation of HCP phase fraction (dropping to ~14% then rising to ~36%).
Compositional inhomogeneity in as-cast or non-homogenized alloys reduces ductility and strain hardening due to localized phase transformation in Fe-enriched regions.
The Fe40Mn40Co10Cr10 single-phase alloy achieves ~95 MPa higher ultimate strength than the equiatomic Co20Cr20Fe20Mn20Ni20 alloy due to enhanced twinning behavior.
The Fe49.5Mn30Co10Cr10C0.5 alloy contains M23C6 carbide nanoparticles with average size 50–100 nm and volume fraction ~1.5 vol.%.
item.mechanism: The authors argue that tuning the free energy difference between FCC and HCP phases via non-equiatomic composition and interstitial addition controls stacking fault energy, enabling sequential activation of deformation mechanisms (dislocation slip, TWIP, TRIP, precipitation, grain boundary strengthening) which collectively enhance strain-hardening capacity and strength–ductility synergy.
item.limitations: High-Mn alloys (>10 at.%) retain Mn-enriched inclusions even after long-term homogenization; long-term annealing at intermediate temperatures can cause chemical segregation; the study focuses primarily on room temperature properties without data on low or elevated temperatures.
item.future_work: The authors propose investigating strength–ductility at low and elevated temperatures, exploring multifunctionalities (corrosion, fatigue, magnetic, hydrogen resistance), introducing shape-memory effects via phase stability design, developing refractory non-equiatomic HEAs (Ti, Nb, Ta, Zr, Hf, V, Mo, W), and screening minor interstitial elements (C, N, B, O) for further performance enhancement.
quotes: This design direction provides ample possibilities for joint activation of a number of strengthening and toughening mechanisms.

Thus-prepared interstitial HEA (referred to as iHEA) was indeed characterized by a combination of various strengthening mechanisms including interstitial and substitutional solid solution, TWIP, TRIP, nanoprecipitates, dislocation interactions, stacking faults, and grain boundaries, leading to twice the tensile strength compared with the equiatomic Co20Cr20Fe20Mn20Ni20 reference HEA while maintain
Indeed, these multiple deformation mechanisms enable significant improvement of the strain-hardening capacity and strength–ductility combination.
